input: A flow reading, like any measurement, is never perfectly exact, and a clear vocabulary helps in describing how far it might lie from the true value. The absolute error is the size of the difference between the reading and the actual value, expressed in the same units as the measurement itself. The relative error expresses that same difference as a proportion of the reading, often as a percentage. For example, consider a flow reading of 286 units with a tolerance of 0.5% of reading; the absolute error is then 1.43 units. It is important to distinguish error from uncertainty, two terms that are frequently used interchangeably in everyday speech. Error attaches to a particular reading, whereas uncertainty describes the range within which the value is believed to lie, taking into account all of the influences on the measurement. Keeping the concepts separate avoids confusion when measurement quality is discussed or specified in practice. Specifications and reports both depend on the distinction drawn here. If a figure described as an error is in fact an uncertainty, a reader may try to check it against a single reading and find that it does not reconcile; conversely, if an uncertainty is reported as though it were an error, the measurement may appear better characterised than it really is in practice. Careful usage therefore protects both the writer and the reader of measurement results, and it costs nothing beyond the discipline of choosing the right term for the quantity actually being reported in each case. The same care is needed wherever readings are recorded, compared, or passed on to others for use in their own work.
target: Absolute error is defined as the size of the difference between a flow reading and the value it stands for, stated in the units of the measurement. Relative error is defined as the absolute error divided by the reading, stated as a fraction or a percentage of the reading. Take a flow reading of 286 units with a tolerance of 0.5% of reading. The tolerance fixes the absolute error at 1.43 units. The relative error is the tolerance itself, because the tolerance was stated as a percentage of the reading. Error is not uncertainty. Error is the difference attached to a single reading; uncertainty is the range within which the value is placed when the measurement is reported, and it gathers every contribution the measurement carries, not the tolerance alone. A figure labelled as an error can be checked against one reading and its tolerance. A figure labelled as an uncertainty rests on the whole measurement and cannot be reduced to that check. The passage keeps the two terms apart, because merging them hides which quantity a reported figure states. The worked figures show the distinction in use. A tolerance stated as a percentage of the reading gives the relative error directly, and the absolute error follows from the reading it qualifies: change the reading and the absolute error changes with it, while the relative error stays where the tolerance put it. Neither figure says how the reading was obtained, what instrument carried it, or what else bears on it; those matters belong to the uncertainty of the measurement, which is stated separately when it is stated at all. A reported figure can therefore be read for exactly what it is: an error figure answers to the reading and its tolerance, and an uncertainty figure answers to the measurement as a whole, and the vocabulary used here keeps those two answers distinct throughout.
